newsitem.title: USA: Do not victimize issuers on yield burning - groups.
newsitem.headline: Do not victimize issuers on yield burning - groups.

text.p: Municipal bond industry representatives said they will press for solutions to the "yield burning" problem that do not victimize issuers when they meet with U.S. Treasury Department's top official on the issue for the first time on Monday.

As reported by Reuters Jan 16, the Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA), National League of Cities, National Association of Bond Lawyers (NABL) and other groups are set to meet at 1100 EST on Jan 27 with Donald Lubick, Treasury's assistant secretary for tax policy.

Representatives of bond lawyers and issuers said in interviews on Friday that they will repeat recommendations they made at a three-hour IRS hearing Jan 15 on the issue when they meet Lubick on Monday.
Lubick is Treasury's top brass on yield burning ever since Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin recused himself on the issue last year because of a possible conflict of interest.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond refinancing deals.

Internal Revenue Service last year stunned localities with a "closing agreement" plan that says issuers can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by paying Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on purchase date, plus interest.

Issuer groups urged IRS January 15 to scrap their voluntary plan and adopt a new one that puts the onus on Wall Street firms that knowingly sold inflated Treasuries to municipalities, and on the few localities, if any, that were aware of the scam.

"These are securities violations," Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for GFOA, said in a telephone interview. "It ought to be securities regulators who are doing something. If there's any way for us to cooperate, we are willing."

But that cooperation does not mean that issuers should supply detailed documents to IRS without a promise that they will not be subject to probes from SEC and IRS, Spain said. "They've got to provide an incentive for us to come in," Spain said.
Amy Dunbar, NABL's chief lobbyist, said, "No one is saying there should be immunity if an issuer knowingly yield burned."
She noted in testimony on the 15th NABL said that Section 6700 of the IRS already gives IRS the ammunition it needs to pursue yield burning violators."
The rule says IRS can fine anyone who aids or abets tax fraud. The fine is $1,000 per denomination, according to bond lawyers.
"We want this taken care of and cleaned up," Spain said. "(But) we don't want to be victimized here. They've got a mess on their hands," she said.
Bond groups will "try to be helpful. The main point is that they should not be penalizing the issuer," Spain said.
